utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody. Good morning, Mr. Sabljica.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Gaynor, although the accused started cross-examining the witness yesterday, upon second thought the Chamber is of the opinion that it would be helpful for you to lead the evidence live in relation to the general methodology of investigation into shelling and sniping, in particular determining angle of descent and determining range of fire in relation to shelling incidents, which appears on pages 14 to 18 of his statement, and the method of investigation in relation to sniping incidents which appears on pages 67 and 69. Given their technical mathematical or geometrical nature, it would be a bit difficult for us to understand what are written in the Rule 92 ter statement without some kind of guidance from the witness. So I wonder whether you can do that right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Certainly, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You would like initially a general explanation of methodology, followed by specifically --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you look at those statements, he refers to sine, cosine or hypotenuse, which I heard during the school days.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And then we'll give our ruling after having heard the -- that in-chief evidence as to how much time the accused should have for his cross-examination. Yes, Mr. Gaynor. It's out of order, but we stopped the cross-examination in the meantime, so I would like you to lead that evidence-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Certainly, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. Sabljica, could you explain, in general, the methodology that you would use in respect of shelling incidents? Just in general terms, first of all, and then I'll ask you some specific questions.

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said yesterday, when analysing a particular photograph with regard to artillery projectiles that came for mortars, we used a particular pattern that we used -- that we called the method of the central axis. When a shell falls on a surface, with its axis it makes an angle that is less than 90 degrees, and when hitting the ground, the body of the shell explodes, and that's when, on the asphalt surface, an ellipsis is made, leaving a different kind of trace, and it goes beyond the center of the ellipsis from where the shell had come from.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat his last sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When this comes together with the center of the ellipsis, an angle is obtained of a certain number of degrees, and then, on the basis of the center of this angle, we determine the direction from which the shell came. On the basis of the angle obtained, a line is marked in the center of this angle, which shows the direction from which the mortar shell came. That is what is done in the case of mortar shells.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, my next question concerns angle of descent. Perhaps you could draw a picture to illustrate your answer, but, first of all: Was it your general practice to calculate the angle of descent in mortar incidents?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I calculated the angle of descent only in one particular case. That was the shelling case at Kosevsko Brdo, as far as I can remember. There is evidence to that effect in my statement. There was some material there. In other cases, we avoided measuring the angle of descent because we did not have adequate equipment for that. If you wish, I can explain that particular case in greater detail, why we did it and for what reason.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I intervene? In the transcript, the witness said "we," not "I," as far as the calculation of the angle is concerned. That can be checked on the recording, "we."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's a subject for you to pursue later on. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. Sabljica, could you explain, first of all, what was the equipment that you lacked which would have been necessary to make an accurate calculation of the angle of descent?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not have special artillery-measuring equipment in order to be able to measure, with precision, the angle of descent of the shell. On one occasion - I'm referring to that case at Kosevsko Brdo - at the request of the investigating judge, we applied a method which is not very precise, and this is what we did: The stabilising fin -- actually, we imagined an axis from that fin, and then we applied classical geometry in order to be able to calculate the angle of descent.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could I ask you at this stage simply to draw a diagram illustrating the elements of classical geometry, as you describe it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That can be done using e-court?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I understand it can, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We can start with a blank page.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Believe me, there is a problem with translation. Mr. Sabljica mentioned this, but it is not in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What is it, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have a problem with the interpretation. I noticed yesterday that my last submissions to the Court were not interpreted properly, and now the witness mentioned the method of the rod. However, that was not reflected in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Sabljica, did you say anything in relation to a rod?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I mentioned a rod. I did not say that that was the method applied, because there is no such law. I said that we used a rod in order to represent this imaginary axis of the projectile or, rather, the stabiliser that was found stuck in the asphalt surface at the point of impact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Karadzic. Yes, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. Sabljica, could you draw the triangle to illustrate the angle of descent and the cosine and the hypotenuse which you've referred to in your previous evidence on this subject?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm going to be speaking as I draw this in order to be clearer. We are going to imagine that this is an asphalt surface [marks], that this is where we found the stabiliser, the tail-fin of the shell. In this case at Kosevsko Brdo, between the remains of this crater that has a certain depth, we got this rod and we calculated this angle, alpha, by setting the length of the shorter ellipsis that is formed around the center of the crater. We're going to mark that with an X [marks]. And we determined the length of this hypotenuse. We're going to mark that with a Y [marks]. And then we calculated the cosinus X through Y, and the angle was obtained, arcus cosinus, X, Y, cosine and sine. [Marks] I have to say that this is rather imprecise in relation to a real piece of artillery-measuring equipment that would make it possible for us to calculate the angle of descent with precision. So our margin of error was plus/minus 10 per cent. I would like to add one more thing. For our report for setting the direction from where the projectile came, this was not that precise at all, because, I repeat, we did not look at that, from which point the projectile had been fired, because for that laser radars and other such equipment are needed too, and that is not feasible. That's the way it was during the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Just to clarify, the diagram which you've just drawn, does Y indicate the length from the surface to the end of the rod you were using; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because it was easy to measure the rod. So its length was well known.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And how did you measure the length from the apex of the triangle to the ground? How did you measure that side?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean, X?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'm actually referring to the third side of the triangle.

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]. The third side was not looked at at all. For the cosine, it is this hypotenuse that is important [indicating].

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: In that case, how did you measure side X?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of the dimensions of the ellipsis that is formed around the crater, itself, which I explained during the explanation of this method, how this irregular ellipsis is formed. So that is done on the basis of the traces that come into existence when the shell falls.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, your evidence, just to clarify this, you determined the angle of descent in respect of one incident only; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because that's what we were asked to do by the investigating judge for that incident. We were not asked to do that for other incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Did you determine the range of fire in respect of the incidents that you investigated?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I repeat, because we had no possibility of doing that because we did not have laser-guided radars. We just said the direction from which the shell had arrived and the type of projectile that had fallen on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: What was the -- what are the relevant factors in determining range of fire, as a general matter?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, the type of artillery piece from which the projectile had been fired. Then, secondly, the charge that had been used, the type of shell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you explain, were you aware in these instances, in the instances which you investigated, of the charge used?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, we could not get that information. It was impossible to determine that, applying the methods that we were using.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you explain, briefly, why it is that the number of charges on the projectile is not possible -- that it is not possible to determine that at the point of impact alone?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because we did not have appropriate equipment or sufficient knowledge to apply certain methods that can be used. As far as I know, it is very difficult to determine which charge was used if you don't have a laser-guided radar to establish the point from where the firing had taken place. Then you can look at the range by using tables; that is to say, the distance from which a mortar fires. In this particular case, it was 120 millimetres. So then you can tell with which kind of charge it gives the best results.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And is it right that in respect of the 120-millimetre, for example, mortar, that you can fire that mortar with zero, one, two, three, four, five, or six charges on it; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This zero is the basic charge of the shell, itself. Additional charges are added, of course, so that the mortar would have a bigger range, depending on the target that is being targeted.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: So the distance that the projectile travels depends very much on the number of charges on the projectile when it is fired; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Inter alia, yes, and, of course, the type of shell that is being used, because a mortar has a small initial velocity. It is used for the direct targeting of particular objectives. As far as I can remember, it is a 7475 mortar that is most productive, the one that was used at the time. It is between 4.700 and 6.750 bullets.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: If you could sign and date the picture on your screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I would ask for that to be admitted, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P1722.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Gaynor, if I can go back to what he said today. Mr. Sabljica, you said - it's page 5, line 23 to 25 - I quote: "I have to say this is imprecise in relation to a real piece of artillery-measuring equipment that would make it possible for us to calculate the angle of descent with precision. So our margin of error was plus/minus 10 per cent." Do you remember that, Mr. Sabljica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In your statement, on page 13, under the subheading of "Accuracy of Determination of Direction of Fire," you said: "Normally, in our reports we would indicate a margin of error that was plus/minus 5 per cent concerning the direction of the shell." So if you can clarify between those differences.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 5 per cent was taken when the direction was established from which the shell had arrived, in terms of cardinal points, right, so if it came from the north, because the method that we used was a lot more exact and precise than the one that I explained in relation to the angle of descent. When applying this method, the margin of error for establishing the angle of descent is higher. That is why it is plus/minus 10 per cent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can you give us a general explanation as to the method you decide the direction of fire, separate from the angle of descent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've already said that, and I will repeat once again. It's the method of the central axis that you use on the basis of the traces that were found at the point of impact. The traces form an irregular ellipse, and then the top points are connected with the center. You get an angle, you draw it, and then you draw a central axis, and it shows the direction from which you assume that the projectile had arrived. Then, with the assistance of a city map and a compass, you determine, first of all, where the position is on the map, and then, in relation to the north, you see how big the angle is, and you have a reserve of plus/minus 5 degrees because of, say, the imprecision in marking the traces on the surface.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sabljica. Back to you, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. Sabljica, could I ask you to draw another diagram, please. In this case, could you mark, first of all, a typical crater pattern from the impact of a mortar, for example, a 120-millimetre mortar?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will idealise this a little bit in order to explain the method. The same picture always emerges on the asphalt when a projectile lands. You have the center of impact [marks], where usually you find the stabiliser of the projectile, in 90 per cent of the cases, and then two irregular ellipses are formed around it [marks] with traces of hot metal -- traces left behind by hot metal [marks]. These are the parts of the shell that fly off when the shell explodes. Our task was to mark these ellipses on the ground and then connect the furthest points of the ellipses with the center of impact and draw a line cutting the angle in half [marks]. And this line would mark the direction from which the projectile had arrived. Sometimes the angle is more acute, sometimes it's more obtuse, depending on the kind of surface the shell landed on, and other things as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: In the picture which you've just described, was it your practice to put down sticks on the ground to indicate the furthest angle in which the traces could be found?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll correct you. We did not stick sticks on the ground. We did not actually push them into the ground, but we laid them on the ground. This is something we did if it was impossible to use chalk because the ground was wet or the chalk would not be sufficiently visible when photographs were taken. In those cases, we would lay down sticks in order to delineate the angle I have just drawn.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And was it your practice, where the ground was dry, to put chalk marks around the traces of impact of shrapnel on the surface to better determine the pattern of the impact?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We almost always used chalk. That was the easiest thing to do, and you could mark the largest number of marks on the ground in order to get the best possible picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'll show you a photograph of that in a moment. In the meantime, could I ask you to sign and date the sketch which you've just marked.

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. That will be Exhibit P1723.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd now like to show you, Mr. Sabljica, a photograph from a file of photo documentation from a shelling incident at Dobrinja, 3B, and the date of the impact was the 1st of June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could I ask for P1699, please, and page 7 of the B/C/S. No need for the English. For the record, this concerns shelling incident G4. Now, if we could enlarge photograph 5, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. Sabljica, if you could explain what we see in photograph 5. First of all, are the traces of the impact marked in chalk in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the traces are marked with chalk, most of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you describe what the three sticks that we see on this photograph -- why they are placed in the locations that they are placed?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are the lines that we got when we connected the irregular ellipse with the center of the explosion. As you can see, we marked all the traces here, and we marked the furthest points of this ellipsis, and then we joined this to the center of the explosion.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sorry, could I just interrupt for a moment. Could you mark with a pen "1," "2," and "3" for the sticks, and explain what "1," "2," and "3" mean?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]. Stick number 1 is one side of the angle, and stick number 2 is the other side of the angle. And you can see under the stick the pole of the ellipse of that wing, and the photograph is incomplete. Probably the other one is there also. And the stick number 3 shows the line dividing the angle in half, the symmetrical line, showing where the projectile arrived from. And the object used to mark it is the tape measure from the toolbox we had with us. And we used the compass to determine the position of the north so that you can read where the projectile arrived from in relation to the north point of the compass.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, in this photograph we see two traces of shrapnel damage, one close to the point of impact and one slightly further away from the point of impact. Are you able to comment on why that is?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two ellipses are created, a smaller one around the center and a second one which is considerably larger. So the traces can be seen at a greater distance from the center and are more visible because the shrapnel goes downwards, in that direction. In the other direction, the shrapnel flies upwards, so there are fewer traces and they're not so visible.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you explain, in this instance, why you put the stick you've marked with "1" in that particular location and why you put the stick marked with "2" in that location? What were the factors determining where, exactly, you placed the stick?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the end points of this ellipsis started from where we put sticks 1 and 2 in relation to the center of the explosion.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: So this photograph doesn't necessarily show all of the shrapnel marks; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: 90 per cent of them can be seen in this photograph because, to the best of my memory, there were no walls or other obstacles nearby where shrapnel could leave traces, in view of the fact that this shell landed on a football field -- football pitch. There was a parking-lot there, and there was a football game going on when this happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could I ask you to sign and date that particular photograph, please?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before I sign, if you allow me, I would like to add that this on-site investigation was carried out after the end of the hostilities in Sarajevo, at the request of the investigating judge and the ICTY, because this occurred in June 1993, at which time I was not working in the police. Mr. Van Hecke and I did it together, and this is an illustration of how the method of the central axis was used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What does another rod with an indication of arrow, which marks as "I" refer to, Mr. Sabljica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is an upside down letter N showing where north is. I will mark it here [marks]. And what you see here marked "C" is a compass which we laid down there so that we could see -- establish the north point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I request that that be admitted, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be done.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P1730.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if we could move, on the same page, to photograph number 6, just below photograph number 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: In this photograph, Mr. Sabljica, could you explain what the sheet of paper is on the ground?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a map of the city of Sarajevo, marking the location where the incident occurred. And we put a compass there to show how we determined what part of town could be suspect as being the place from where the projectile arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you simply mark the map with the letter M?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And for the record, just indicate the direction of fire as determined in this instance.

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]. I will mark it with the number 3, as in the previous photograph. So this rod marks the direction of the fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it the map should be located in parallel with the indication of north, but this picture is taken just for an introductory purpose.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, the map also has to be -- has to be turned in such a way that the points of the compass are properly aligned, north-south, east-west. This is why the map is turned in this way. This happened in Dobrinja, so we had to turn the map in such a way that the north end of the map would be pointing to the actual north in real life.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could draw a line in the middle of that map in the direction it was laid. I see it's not parallel to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: No, what you've done is you've orientated the map in the same way that you would if you were on a map-reading exercise, so that north is, as it were, indicated on the map, but we can't necessarily see it. So the map is simply orientated to the direction of north and the direction of fire. Is that what you did?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, precisely so. I will mark the edges of the map here [marks] so that you can get a complete picture. The map had to be orientated towards the north so that we could establish where the shell came from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'll leave it there. Yes. Carry on, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes. Could that photograph --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you sign and date that photograph, please, Mr. Sabljica?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If north can be marked on the map, itself, because the edge of the map is not parallel with the marking of the north on the ground. These two lines would intersect at some point, the edge of the map and the rod on the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I answer that question? The map is oriented towards the north. It cannot be parallel with the rod because Dobrinja, in relation to north in Sarajevo, is a little to the south-west. When you are orientating a map, you have to use a compass and orientate the map in the direction of geographical north, and the place on the map that you are interested in has to be aligned with the actual place in town. So it can't be completely parallel. This an ordinary sort of map that you can buy in bookshops in town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Sabljica, do you see the fourth rod you indicated, which would indicate the direction of the north? Could you mark -- could you circle the letter N down there? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. I will put an arrow there and mark it with an "N" for "North" [marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My question was whether that direction should be parallel to the direction that the map was laid. Could you indicate northbound on that map? So my question is: Two lines will be parallel if you draw on that map indicating the north?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. So this picture is not ideal because what is crucial is the needle on the compass which has to be parallel with the line that I drew down there [marks]. I may not have delineated the map very precisely on this picture with the red marker because it's not really clearly visible on the photograph. However, the compass needle indicates north and is parallel to the line I have drawn there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Also, you have to take into account the deviation, the difference between magnetic north and true north.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course. That's why we always had a plus/minus 5-degree tolerance in all our calculations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could I request that that be admitted, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is this not -- no, sorry. Yes, picture number 6 will be admitted. Marked what?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1731, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And very briefly, if we could go to the previous page of this 65 ter number, please. If we can focus in on photograph 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Is that an picture of the crater location before the chalk marks were applied?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is it. And here you can see the measurement rod, measuring the dimensions of the ellipse. If you like, I will draw the ellipse to make it clearer.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]. We have two irregular ellipses, one around the crater and a larger one. This is, more or less, the center of the explosion [marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you mark the axis -- for illustrative purposes, could you mark which axis represents the direction of fire?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The photograph is not complete. I don't see all the traces here. But if I were to draw the angles, I think it's easier to see on the next picture. In this picture, we only measured the dimensions of the ellipse, without marking the traces.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I understand. So the white rod we see in this photograph is simply a measuring tape to measure the dimensions of the ellipse and not the direction of fire or anything like that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's a measure band from the tool kit of the forensic technician, showing the dimensions of the traces on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: If you could sign and date that, please.

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be admitted as Exhibit P1732.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And finally on this subject, if we could move to photograph number 4 on the same page.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Here, Mr. Sabljica, we see again the three rods, which you described in your earlier evidence, and the direction north on the top of the photograph; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is photograph number 4, which is similar to photographs 5 and 6, but taken from a different angle. Here we see the direction of the north. We see the sides of the angle. We see the poles of the larger ellipse, and the rod with red markings indicates the direction of fire [marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Which you've marked with the letter D; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The direction, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: If you could sign and date that, please.

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Exhibit P1733.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Finally on this subject, Mr. Sabljica: Is it correct that once you've measured the direction of fire at impact location, it's not, in fact, necessary to have a map at the impact location, provided you know where the impact location was; that you can then look at a map later in your office and, with your data concerning direction of fire, you can establish back at your office the direction from which the projectile arrived?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We usually had a map with us, always, so that we could establish on the spot from which part of town or from which part of the territory the shell might have arrived. But we never indicated a precise location in our reports or named an army that might have fired the projectile.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I want to move now to the question of sniping, and I want to ask you a few questions about your methodology there. I want to ask you, first of all, about the sniping of trams. Where you -- where a tram was sniped, had been hit by fire, could you describe briefly your overall approach to investigating those kinds of incidents?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same forensic team, headed by the investigating judge, with ballistics experts and forensic technicians, arrived on the spot. First, they would mark the traces on the tram, the entry and exit openings, their dimensions, their positions. And then equipment would be used, a rope, glass tubes, and a small optical device, which would help us to determine the potentially suspect facilities from where the bullet might have arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could I ask you just to draw a diagram, a simple explanatory diagram, indicating how you might determine the direction of fire in a tram sniping incident?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will idealise this a little bit again. [Marks]. Let's assume that this is a tram. These are the wheels [marks]. This is the outer wall of the tram [marks], and there is an entry opening, and in most cases we also found an exit opening [marks]. Then you would insert a glass or metal rod through these two openings or you would pull a rope through and pull it tight [marks]. And then with the help of an optical device that we constructed, you would determine the optical sights direction, showing where the bullet might have been fired from. And it's easy to calculate the angle of entry in relation to the ground, the line on the ground [marks], so that you could calculate this angle here.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you briefly mark, with the number 1, the entry point, with number 2, the exit point, in this diagram?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: What was the nature of the optical device which you used?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was made for us in the Ministry of the Interior so that we could use it. It's like a rather sophisticated binoculars so that we could have optical visibility through the holes made in the side of the tram.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: How, exactly, would you measure the angle which you have indicated in this diagram?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Using geometry, as I explained in the case of shells landing. You can take the thickness of the tram side. You have the hypotenuse, and then you can calculate alpha X through Y [marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Perhaps -- thank you. If you could -- just to the left of the diagram of the tram, could you simply draw a triangle indicating the entry point, the exit point, the angle of fire, and --

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]. 1 is the entry opening and the other one is the exit opening. Then this is the thickness of the wall of the tram [marks], which is always known. Then this is the length of this thread that we used [marks]. And then the alpha angle was determined on the basis of the formula that I already wrote up. It was a lot simpler and more precise in relation to shells, because that rod method, if we could call it that, is not exactly precise and it cannot exactly determine what we need.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: In the diagram, we've just noted X is the width of the wall of the tram, and Y is the distance between the entry point and the exit point; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: X is a dimension that shows the thickness of the wall of the tram. So it's not the length of the side of the tram. It is a cross-section of the wall of the tram, if you were looking at the tram from that point of view, looking at its thickness, as it were.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And Y is the distance between the entry point and the exit point; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you. If you could sign and date that, please.

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I request that that be admitted, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1734, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Did you investigate sniping incidents which did not concern the sniping of trams?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: In those instances, what was your methodology for determining the origin of fire?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same methods, because in all cases it was easy to link at least two cases of damage through a particular surface. I remember a particular case in an apartment in this building near Vrbanja Bridge. I can't remember exactly what the name of the street is. There was damage on the windows, a window that had been protected with a very thin wooden board, and it was very easy to establish it because we used the same method. The method of sighting, we called it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, could you explain whether the method of sighting enables you to determine only the direction of fire or whether it also enables you to determine the probable origin of fire?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The direction of fire, but also, more precisely, the area from which it could have come, roughly. It gave a higher possibility of assuming where this had come from, because this optical device helped us considerably in tracking the suspicious part of town, if I can put it that way, on the basis of the measurements that we had done.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you explain, briefly, how, exactly, you would use the optical device to determine the origin of fire?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This optical device was lightly fixed to this metal or glass tube that was put through the opening, and then if you looked through it, you could see the potentially suspicious building, in terms of the direction from which the projectile had arrived. When you looked through this optical device, you got a closer image, as it were. It seemed closer than if viewed with the naked eye only.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, when you refer to potentially suspicious buildings, were you under any pressure of any kind to identify any particular buildings as potentially suspicious?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course not. We can go back to my statement yesterday, when I said that in this one case of the tram, there was no optical visibility between that green building, if we're going to call it that, and the tram that had been hit, because the tram driver did not take the tram back to the original place. There was no pressure, and I specifically did not wish to feel pressured in any way and exposed to certain suggestions, possible suggestions, made by other members of the team.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Where you were not able to return a tram to the location where it had been hit, what was your methodology for determining direction and origin of fire?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that case, we just conducted measurements. We calculated the angles, but we did not conduct classical sighting to see from where this could have arrived. In our findings, we did not state that at all. We said that it had come from, we assume, the left side, in relation to the movement of the tram, the trajectory was such and such, the angles in relation to the side of the tram are such and such, and in that way we completed our statement. We could have seen that in one of my findings yesterday. I think that the late Medjedovic and I signed those findings. We looked at them yesterday. And one of the colleagues claimed that it was skyscraper number 4, and I said that is not written in our findings. We could not have established the exact facility or building from where it had come because the tram could not have been returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Why, in certain circumstances, were you not able to return the tram to the location where it was struck by fire?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In one case, the tram had broken down because the firing had damaged it. And, you know, in that situation, in a situation of war, it is very difficult to do this kind of work and to return a vehicle to the exact spot where it was. And also there was fear. People were simply afraid of taking the tram back to the same site because no one can guarantee that you will not be fired at again.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: During periods of cease-fire, did you consider it safe to return a tram always to the location where it had been struck?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I specifically never felt safe in Sarajevo. We tried to work - how should I put it? - normally, professionally, in a very difficult situation. Even at times of cease-fire, nobody could guarantee that fire would not be opened yet again.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't know if you wish me to ask anything further on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gaynor. It was very helpful to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, we considered your request regarding the amount of time for your cross-examination. The Chamber is of the view, in light of the additional evidence-in-chief, you can focus more on the relevant issues, so the Chamber believes that seven hours would be more than sufficient for you to cross-examine this witness. And Judge Morrison has some further words for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, this is designed to assist. Although it's the case that on cross-examination a witness is at large as to relevant and admissible questions within the parameters of Rule 90(H), it seems to the Trial Chamber that the better course for you is to attempt to restrain yourself to the topics arising directly out of the written and oral testimony given in chief, and, in particular, to avoid the unnecessary reading of documents which, if translated, could be read by all parties and already form part of the court record, if and when admitted as exhibits. This is particularly germane when you have a record of previous testimony and cross-examination that is already available to you and the Trial Chamber and enables you to highlight any inconsistencies without the necessity of re-running every topic. It's also important when you know in advance how long you have. The purpose of limiting cross-examination, as it has been with limiting examination-in-chief, is not to place artificial limits, but to create a basis for focusing upon the really important matters that go to the indictment against you, as well as attempting to make the trial, as a whole, more expeditious, an expeditious trial being part of the matrix of fair trial procedure. If the Chamber considers that the original limitation is too constricting, then it will, as it already has in many cases, allow more time when good cause is demonstrated. As Mr. Robinson knows, the effect of examination and cross-examination of witnesses is an art, predicated by concision and preparation, so please take advice from your qualified lawyers. Quantity does not equate with quality, and please bear that in mind, because the Trial Chamber certainly does. Note in particular, though, that the Trial Chamber is not attempting to bar any relevant topic, nor prevent any aspect of a proper defence. On the contrary, it's attempting to make the Defence more focused, and by doing so, make it more precise and of better forensic quality. That can only be to your advantage.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellencies, for the additional time and your well-intentioned suggestions. Of course, I shall --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll have a break before you start, if it is convenient. And before that, I have one thing to deal with with respect to the accused's request dated 27th September 2010, in which Mr. Karadzic requested the presence of Defence expert Dr. Subotic in the courtroom during the testimony of six Prosecution witnesses: John Hamill, Emir Turkusic, KDZ477, KDZ485, Per Anton Brennskag, and Thorbjorn Overgard. The Prosecution did not oppose this request, and in light of the anticipated technical nature of these witnesses' testimony, we will grant the request to have Dr. Subotic present in the courtroom during the testimony of these six witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If I could also deal with one housekeeping matter. Yesterday, the Prosecution filed a second motion for a video-link testimony of Dr. Youssef Hajir, and having reviewed the medical information, we want to advise the Chamber that we don't oppose that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then it will be granted, then. Thank you. We'll have a break for about 20 minutes. We'll resume at 10.35.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Sabljica.

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Have you gotten used to these early sunsets, or does the sun set early in our part of the world as well?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a bit unusual. The sun rises earlier in our part of the world now. I was here all week because I was hoping to get this done by now, but, anyway, I'm used to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you are now fresh, in terms of this morning's direct examination, let me deal with that. When you spoke of deviations from the bearing of -- from the azimuth, the bearing of fire, you said "plus/minus 5 degrees"?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And when you spoke of the angle of descent, you spoke of plus/minus 10 per cent; right?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was actually referring to degrees, plus/minus 10 degrees. Perhaps there is a mistake in translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That's what I wanted to look at, whether we're talking about degrees or percentage points in that case. Thank you. So we've resolved that. Tell me, do you recall that in Sarajevo, one line followed another, the line of conflict or separation? They followed each other like a red-and-white pen, a two-coloured pen; right?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to maps or are you talking about reality?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Reality.

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I can confirm that. In most cases, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that between the point of fall of descent of a shell and the Muslim line, there is quite a bit of space in which there can be artillery pieces?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President. In respect of these questions, could Mr. Karadzic focus his questions on a specific part of Sarajevo in order to clarify the question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Karadzic, could you reformulate your question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I thought that we had established that the lines, the Serb and Muslim lines, followed each other, and that this was around the inner-city, and that it went through the inner-city.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If something fell on Muslim territory between the actual site or scene where this took place and then the Muslim lines, and then the Serb lines, there is a certain space, isn't there?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before I respond, I would just like to draw your attention to something. I don't know what kind of Muslim lines you are referring to. Who are these Muslims? So far, your terminology has been fair that has been adopted in this Tribunal. I would kindly ask you to use the terms "the Army of Republika Srpska" and "the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina" for the two conflicting parties, because this insults my national feelings. I don't want you to consider me as some kind of Muslim militia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I will respect that. But Serbs accounted for less than 1 per cent, only .7 per cent of the personnel of that army. So between the points of impact and the line of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, there is a certain space that is controlled by the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, isn't there?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean between the lines of the Army of Republika Srpska and the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, there was no-man's land; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: No, I'll be a bit more specific. Say we have a site or a scene where something took place, and then we have an area that's under the control of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and then there's a line of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. There's a little bit of no-man's land or none whatsoever, and then there's the Serb line and then there's Serb territory; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, please -- now we're going to move on to what you kindly clarified in relation to snipers. How thick is the wall of the tram?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, between the external and internal part, taking into account these three layers, there's between 12 and 15 centimetres.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So that's how thick the wall is?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because it is a sandwich consisting of thin metal sheeting, and in between there's a small area filled with air.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How long is that little tube that you used to establish the direction?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 30 centimetres.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How thick is it?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the set, we had several of these small tubes, depending on the type and calibre of ammunition that was used. That is to say that this was specifically made for this purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What else did you have in respect of this kind of equipment? What else did you use when measuring that angle?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: When measuring the angle, we used the mathematics I displayed; that is to say, a classical protractor, these tubes that helped us fix the entry-and-exit openings, to link up several points along the trajectory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You didn't use anything else?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This optical device as well that only helped us with the sighting to get the image closer to us. It didn't have any protractors on it. It was simply like a set of binoculars, a bit more sophisticated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that in order to determine this angle, what is of crucial importance is that the only cathetus that you worked with should be parallel with the surface or the ground; that is to say, that it should be impeccably horizontal?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree, when measuring the angle of descent of the ammunition in respect of the plane of the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you use a level, then?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I omitted to mention that. We did have this small level in the set that the crime scene officer had. You will probably have an opportunity of examining one of them too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who invented this optical device?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We sent a request to the head of our department, stating that we needed this kind of device. I don't know exactly who made it, but we got one. I think that it was made in the factory called Zrak. You're familiar with it, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That's what I thought. But tell me, what was the zoom like of that particular device?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sixteen times, up to sixteen times, so you had a rather good survey in relation to classical binoculars that are being used for whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I see. And how thick was it?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean, how thick?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The optical device, itself, how thick was it? Could it enter the opening?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it could not enter the opening. It would be fixed on this metal tube, the little metal tube. So the ocular would coincide with the center of that tube, and then from higher up you could look at it very easily. It's similar to a periscope, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that these optical instruments -- or, rather, when air goes from one setting to another, there are certain aberrations. The aberration of light, did you take that into account in respect of this optical device?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with that refraction of light, yes. We did not have that kind of equipment, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that determining this with a rope, because, after all, a rope is flexible, it's a bit imprecise, it's the wrong way to do it, it's too much of a make-shift thing, as it were? You said that when the rope had been tightened, it could go through both openings?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The rope was only used as a support, you know. We would tighten it and fix it pretty well, so it was tense, so that this tube that went through the openings, depending on the calibre of the ammunition used, could be fixed so that we could view things as specifically as possible. It's not that the rope was just taken through just like that. It's not that it wasn't fixed firmly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that when a device is that sensitive, like this optical device is -- actually, has it been tested anywhere for these particular purposes?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't respond to that question because I don't know. We received it at our request. I don't know whether they had tested it previously. At any rate, we used it for magnifying the image of the area that we were looking at, nothing else. We didn't use it for any kind of specific measurements.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that if there is this kind of a very sensitive optical device, it is of crucial importance to establish the exact position where the tram had been when it was hit by this particular ammunition?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, and I have already stated that. If we were unable to bring the tram back, we did not specify where the bullet had come from.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that even centimetres are important here, that several centimetres' difference in the position of the tram would create a huge difference in the angle?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't link this up with the angle, but rather with the suspect facility from which the shots were fired. Yes, I agree, certainly if a tram moved even a few centimetres, it would create a completely different picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was it easy, then, to bring the tram back and establish the precise place where the tram was when the bullet hit it?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course it wasn't easy, and you have already heard this. The tram would be brought back according to witness statements, and the best witness was the driver. The circumstances prevailing at the time dictated what we could do. We always insisted on trying to bring the tram back to the exact position where it was when it was hit, but I do agree that this was very difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your kind conversation with Defence representatives, you stated that in order to establish the type of projectile, you had to have not just pieces of shrapnel, but also something that would identify it precisely; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. And for this reason, we formed an opinion only if we found some identifying parts, such as the stabiliser, for example, which can tell you a great deal about the type of projectile. If we did not find anything like that, then we did not express an opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I forgot to ask you, who in your team dealt with this optical device? Who was in charge of it, so to speak? I don't mean the name of the person. I mean, what kind of expert was it?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was only we from ballistics, the late Stanko, the late Cavcic, Medjedovic and I.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember whether, in addition to the entry-and-exit openings in the tram wall, entry-and-exit wounds were also investigated in the case of entry/exit wounds; do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware of that, but it was not us who did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I draw your attention to the incident in Livanjska Street on the 8th of November, 1994. I can't say what number it is on the F list, but I do have this material. You attended that on-site investigation on the 8th of November, did you not? I'm sorry, it's list G. It's not in the indictment, but it's a well-known incident.

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were two incidents in Livanjska Street, and I attended both. So I know what you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How do you explain the fact that the investigating judge did not attend the investigation?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall the investigating judge being absent. Can you tell me what incident you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The one that happened on the 8th of November, 1994.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If it will assist, can we have 65 ter 09678.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: At the time, it was like this: There were two shells. One landed at 1525 and the other one at 1725. UNPROFOR established that the first arrived from the territory of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I'll tell you why I don't like saying that; because we are also Bosnia-Herzegovina and now we have a common army, so it's easier for the Chamber to understand about the two sides. But let's continue. UNPROFOR established that the first arrived from the territory of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that there was a misunderstanding between the police, the local police or the police of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and UNPROFOR's investigators. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall a shelling incident when we worked together with a team of Frenchmen, I think, and we agreed about the direction, but they used tables belonging to a NATO mortar of 82 millimetres which had a far shorter range than our 81- or 82-millimetre mortars had. And I personally gave the French officer, when we came back to our office, the tables for the 82-millimetre mortar from the library of the JNA, and that's the rules you have going with the artillery pieces. I remember that, but I don't recall whether the investigating judge was there or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at e-court. In the second paragraph, it says that the judge felt it was not necessary for him to go on the spot. Do you agree -- did you see the judge there?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not. And, well, as this is what the official report says, I can only agree with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that a side that was accused or suspected would not like to have this investigation done without the presence of a judge, in our system, at least?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I think this is part of the record, so it need not be admitted. Who was in charge of the investigation on that day; do you recall? You can look at the list.

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think, in that case, it was Mr. Dragan Miokovic, because in the Criminal Sector, he would be the team leader.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. There were victims in this incident, were there not?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A 15-year-old girl was killed. It's recorded here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that this would require the presence of the investigating judge, even more than the previous fact, as we mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I agree.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. It can be taken off the screen now. It's part of the documents tendered by the OTP. Has this been admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, this has been admitted as Exhibit P1704.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In your statement of the 19th of November, 1995, you remembered that there was a misunderstanding with UNPROFOR and that you wanted UNPROFOR to be on the spot when you were conducting an investigation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. As a rule, we always insisted that the gentlemen from UNPROFOR be present.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 20874, please, to jog our memories, 65 ter, and it's page 3 in the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: For people who are not from Sarajevo, when you speak of Kosevo Hill, you're also referring to Livanjska Street; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's Livanjska Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can I draw your attention to where you say: "We immediately agreed as regards the direction of fire. On the day of the incident, UNPROFOR did not conduct -- they left the spot without conducting an investigation. And the next day, we returned with UNPROFOR ..." So where was the misunderstanding?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The misunderstanding was about the type of artillery piece that was used, because, as I've just said, the UNPROFOR officer used tables belonging to a NATO weapon which was not of the same calibre as our mortar and had a far shorter range. Later on, I personally gave him the tables. That was the difference. I don't think that we expressed an opinion as to the location from where the shell had arrived, but we only established the general direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So the tables would be important in establishing the range?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were using tables belonging to a quite different type of mortar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I have to wait for the interpretation. Do you remember that Mr. Miokovic asked that the police secure the site, and stressed that UNPROFOR should not be allowed access to the site?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm really not aware of that. You'll probably have to ask Dragan that. He'll probably testify. I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's see whether it's on this page.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 65 ter 10426?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Before we move on, Mr. President, could the statement of the witness, dated 19th November 1995, be admitted, the one that he's just been shown and that he's commented upon?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't see any problem. That will be admitted as --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is cross-examination now, so it's up to the Defence to tender documents, I think, as a rule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, he's right. But to save time, he can raise it in his redirect. I'll leave it to redirect. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have -- oh, yes. Can we have page 3. Yes, this it, the first paragraph in the Serbian language. It's probably where it says: "As a result of the conclusions at that meeting ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you look at that, and: "The policeman who was there told me that they had informed UNPROFOR of the event and they were expecting someone to attend."

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read it, but this is not my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You're right, it's not your statement. It's Mr. Miokovic's statement. And just a moment. Did you see the second part of the first sentence, that they should not allow -- let anyone, and UNPROFOR, in particular, to enter the site?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but that's Dragan's statement. Why are you asking me this?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I just want to establish the facts about an investigation that you participated in. You did not issue this order, but that's what the situation was. I think this is on the record. Do you remember that that same evening, UNPROFOR held a press conference --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The question wasn't whether it was your order, but whether you were aware of such instruction or order, Mr. Sabljica.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, as I said, I was not aware of it. I did not have any information to the effect that Dragan had banned the entry of UNPROFOR. The ballistics team and the criminal forensic team always wanted UNPROFOR to be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, that's what prompted me to demonstrate that the team leader was not of the same opinion as the rest of the team. Do you remember that on that day, UNPROFOR held a press conference?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we scroll down a little bit? It says: "On that day, at a press conference held by UNPROFOR at 2000 hours, a spokesman said to the journalist that the Bosnian police had not allowed them to carry out ..." And can we have the next page, please. "... an investigation. On that same evening, our minister of the interior passed an order to prepare the report because it was requested by the Presidency, and I did so."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember -- are you aware that they held a press conference and that they had been prevented from carrying out an investigation, and they said that?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had no electricity and I was not able to watch television, so I was not aware of this. And this is the first time I have seen this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you aware at the time that Miokovic was required to hand in a report on the same day?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because as for us ballistics people, Miokovic did not make us hurry with our reports. We dealt with this very seriously, we wanted to finish everything on time, and again insisting that UNPROFOR had to attend, if they could, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could it happen, then, that Mr. Miokovic had handed in the report without your findings?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Findings -- without our findings and without our knowledge, either. However, I really don't know. You will have to ask him that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like to ask you to clarify the question of the Finnish tables a bit. You say in this statement: "From November 1995, I saw that the Finnish mortar tables explained that they used maximum charges. When we looked at that, we realised that the Finnish shells only corresponded to the second or third in our tables where we have six possible charges." If necessary, I will call this up.

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall that. It was a lot less than the 72 millimetres, the one that was used in our theatre of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, basically, it didn't seem to be very important because the charge is not relevant for setting the distance; right?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now, what about this statement of Mr. Miokovic's? Are we going to admit it today or -- we have a problem with the transcript. I agreed with the witness that this dispute with UNPROFOR was not important [as interpreted] because a charge is not important for a set -- here, it says that the charge is not important, but I'm saying that it is important for setting the distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could the witness please confirm that, that it wasn't that important because -- the charge is important for setting the distance, and you didn't set it, and they didn't set it either?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Charge is relevant for setting the distance. That is what the transcript should say.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now have 1D02264.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you say you are tendering the statement by Miokovic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender it because it refers to the same things that the witness is familiar with. However, I know what your practice is, so I'm asking you whether you would be willing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: When I said there would be no problem, I thought it was this witness's statement. Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes. Could we go briefly into private session, please, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. As a sign of goodwill from the Defence, we give our consent to admit Mr. Sabljica's statement from November 1995. That's what the Prosecution asked for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that will be done as well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be Exhibit P1735.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I believe that this is from the UN. It is a document that says, on page 9 -- 983 should be the last digits. There should be a map that UNPROFOR had inserted, and I hope that you will be familiar with it. 983 should be the last digits in the ERN number.

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have 975 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It is page 9 in relation to the page on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I please have that on my screen, that page?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, here it is. We've all been waiting for it. Are you familiar with this map that UNPROFOR attached in relation to this incident?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this is the first time I see this map.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you see here that according to their firing tables, a shell has eight charges, not four?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So the true misunderstanding with them was with regard to the place from which it had been fired; right?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I really did not discuss that place with them because we were not establishing that. We were establishing the type of weapon from which the shell had been fired. They compiled this report on the basis of those tables of theirs, I assume. So that place was not the subject of our discussions, because neither they nor we were in a position to establish it exactly, because they did not have laser-guided radars either and similar modern equipment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. That will considerably shorten our examination with regard to this incident. Can this map be admitted, the entire document, the entire document under this number 1D02264?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D738, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What happened in relation to this incident at 1725 hours? Were the difficulties the same and were the results the same?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall. I think that we discussed the first incident more. I don't think that this one was referred to, but I would like to see the report.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we then have 65 ter 10437. That's the English version, 10437. Could we have that just so that you can see the actual site. Could you please turn it 180 degrees. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that now? The direction was being set here; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that the angle of descent was not being determined here?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it wasn't in this case. But in this other case that I mentioned, we did calculate the angle of descent, in another case at Kosevsko Brdo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Not going into the accuracy of the methodology in relation to the measuring of the crater and the 82-millimetre shell, on the basis of an angle established in such a way in this first case, would the firing tables determine a range?

utterances.speaker: MIRZA SABLJICA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that could be taken into consideration. However, I repeat, once again, we did not measure the angles because they were not relevant for us for establishing where the shell had come from. So we tried to use a method that would be as exact and precise as possible for setting the origin of fire. You have the tables for calculating angles of descent. After all, that is science, these firing tables, and quite a bit of effort was made to draw them up when manufacturing and examining every artillery piece.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
